rv.q: An Eye-Opening Experience: In Brian Friel’s play, a blind woman has her sight restored by surgery, only to see that her life and relationships aren’t what they once seemed.

Molly Sweeney is so carefully understated as it proceeds on its determined course that even viewers with 20/20 eyesight may not notice that its encouragement to acknowledge “blindsight” includes a moving one that whispers, “See this play about sight and its many underappreciated manifestations.
The Keen Company's revival directed by Jonathan Silverstein makes a persuasive case for a work that many critics have said succeeds more effectively as a book than as a play.
Not Much to See, but a Lot to Listen to, in Molly Sweeney: Brian Friel's play about a woman who regains her sight gets a Keen Company revival.
For anyone who might have wondered why a blind person might not so readily benefit from being given sight, Molly Sweeney can be an eye-opener.

The longer the characters talk, despite their frankness and eloquence, the more Molly Sweeney suffers from flagging energy; it's a prose piece for the theatre, and it runs out of breath long before it is over.
All in all, this production sails across the surface of the tale, when what Mr. Friel offered was a chance to go deep.
Even with good acting, a play told entirely in monologues can be difficult to make lively.

cn.t: Friel's monologue-driven play about restored sight divides critics: some praise its quiet power and evocative prose, while others find the static format talks itself into a standstill despite strong performances.
